quiz.q: What happens to code under a `#[cfg(...)]` attribute whose condition is false for this build?
options: It runs but is wrapped in an implicit `if false`
It is not compiled at all — as if it were deleted
It compiles but prints a warning every time it runs
It runs only in debug builds
quiz.explain: `#[cfg(...)]` is evaluated at compile time. A false condition means the item is never compiled in, not skipped at runtime.

quiz.q: Which `#[cfg(...)]` condition is true only when compiling with `cargo test`?
options: #[cfg(debug_assertions)]
#[cfg(test)]
#[cfg(target_os = "test")]
#[cfg(feature = "test")]
quiz.explain: `#[cfg(test)]` is true specifically when the crate is being compiled for testing, keeping test-only code out of normal binaries.

quiz.q: You write `#[cfg(feature = "json")]` in your code but never add `json` to `[features]` in Cargo.toml. What happens?
options: Cargo automatically declares the feature for you
It's a compile error immediately
The code is silently excluded forever, since the feature can never be turned on, and modern Cargo warns about it
The feature defaults to enabled
quiz.explain: An undeclared feature can never be enabled, so the gated code is permanently compiled out. Modern Cargo also emits an `unexpected cfg condition value` warning.

quiz.q: What does `optional = true` on a Cargo dependency do?
options: Makes the dependency's version requirement optional
Prevents the dependency from being compiled in unless something enables it (typically via a matching feature)
Downloads the dependency lazily at runtime
Makes the dependency's API calls return Option instead of the real type
quiz.explain: `optional = true` means the dependency is only compiled in when a feature (usually `dep:name` in a `[features]` entry) turns it on — otherwise it's left out entirely.

quiz.q: In `[features] json = ["dep:serde_json"]`, what does the `dep:` prefix accomplish that plain `"serde_json"` would not?
options: It enables the serde_json dependency without also creating a public feature literally named serde_json
It marks serde_json as a dev-dependency
It pins serde_json to a specific version
It has no effect — dep: and no prefix are identical
quiz.explain: Without `dep:`, Cargo also creates an implicit public feature named after the dependency itself, which is usually not intended. `dep:name` enables the dependency directly.

quiz.q: Two crates in the same dependency graph both depend on `logging-lib`. One enables its `colors` feature; the other doesn't request it either way. What happens in the final build?
options: Each crate gets its own separately-compiled copy of logging-lib, with different features
The build fails because of a feature conflict
logging-lib is compiled once with `colors` enabled, since features are additive/unioned across the whole graph
colors is enabled only for the crate that requested it
quiz.explain: Cargo builds each dependency once per build with the union of every feature any crate in the graph requested — features are additive, not per-crate.

quiz.q: Why should a Cargo feature only ever add capability, never change existing behavior in a conflicting way?
options: Because Cargo compiles a separate copy of the crate for every feature combination
Because features are unioned across the whole dependency graph, so one crate's needs can't be isolated from another's in the same build
Because features are resolved at runtime, not compile time
Because rustc rejects any feature that changes behavior
quiz.explain: Since features unify per build rather than per crate, a feature that changes behavior (instead of only adding to it) can silently affect a completely different crate that happens to share the same dependency.

quiz.q: What's a risk of never testing your crate with `--no-default-features`?
options: The crate won't compile at all without default features
Code behind non-default features can silently rot, since it's never actually exercised
Cargo will refuse to publish the crate
It has no real risk — default features are always identical to no features
quiz.explain: If your own builds always include the default features, feature-gated code paths outside that default combination can break without anyone noticing until a user hits them.

flashcards.back: It's an if-statement the compiler evaluates before your program exists. If the condition is false, the item is not compiled in at all — it's gone, not just skipped.

flashcards.front: Name three common #[cfg(...)] conditions besides feature checks.
flashcards.back: #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] (or macos/windows), #[cfg(test)] (true only under cargo test), and #[cfg(debug_assertions)] (true in debug builds, false in --release).

flashcards.front: How do you declare a Cargo feature, and how do you check it in code?
flashcards.back: Declare it in Cargo.toml under [features], e.g. `json = []`. Check it in code with `#[cfg(feature = "json")]`.

flashcards.front: How do you make a dependency opt-in behind a feature?
flashcards.back: Mark the dependency `optional = true`, then add a feature that enables it via `dep:` syntax, e.g. `json = ["dep:serde_json"]`.

flashcards.front: What does the `dep:` prefix in a feature's dependency list do?
flashcards.back: It enables the named optional dependency without also implicitly creating a separate public feature with that same name.

flashcards.front: Are Cargo features additive or exclusive across a dependency graph?
flashcards.back: Additive. Each dependency is compiled once per build with the union of every feature any crate in the graph enabled — there's no per-crate isolation.

flashcards.front: Why must a feature never change existing behavior in a conflicting way?
flashcards.back: Because features are unioned across the whole build, a behavior-changing feature turned on by one crate would silently affect every other crate sharing that dependency in the same build.

flashcards.front: What warning does modern Cargo give for an undeclared feature checked with #[cfg(feature = "...")]?
flashcards.back: `unexpected cfg condition value` — and the gated code is permanently excluded, since a feature that was never declared can never be turned on.
